en: Chapter on Kalpas:
Verses composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of Daci’en Monastery.
The sequence and numerical measure of the kalpas: formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, along with their beginnings and ends.
The other three [aeons] are not fixed and cannot be compared; therefore, they are discussed in terms of their duration based on the *sthiti-kalpa* (abiding aeon).
First, sentient beings are born in Jambudvīpa; at the conclusion of the *vivarta-kalpa* (formation aeon), this marks the beginning of the *sthiti-kalpa*.
At that time, human lifespan was immeasurable, until it reached ten years, marking the end of the *apacaya-kalpa* (decreasing aeon).
And after a hundred years, it decreases by one; eighty-four thousand years is the maximum.
From that point, the sons' years double those of their fathers, ascending again to eighty-four thousand years.
One increase and one decrease constitute one kalpa; when twenty such kalpas are completed, the abiding kalpa ends.
This very period of abiding is called the Bhadrakalpa; among its twenty eons, it is the ninth.
During the periods of sixty thousand, forty thousand, and twenty thousand years, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa appeared.
When the human lifespan was one hundred years, Śākyamuni appeared. When the human lifespan was three hundred thousand years, there was famine.
In the seventh year, on the seventh day of the seventh month, the full term ends; many will perish through the accumulation of bones and the manipulation of schemes.
At the age of twenty, diseases shall invade; the calamities of the seventh day of the seventh month shall finally conclude.
When one reaches the age of ten [in the subsequent cycle], weapons of war shall arise, and for seven days and seven nights, people shall slaughter and wound one another.

A small remainder of people shall not be entirely extinguished; through fear of calamities they cultivate merit, increasing their lifespan and doubling the years of their sons, which increase by eighty thousand. From that point, during the kalpa of decrease, Maitreya shall arise;
until the fifteenth kalpa of decrease, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas will appear.
Then, at the end of the kalpa of abiding, when the Tathāgata Louti is about to appear in the world,
during the final period of the kalpa of increase alone, people grow weary of worldly pleasures and cultivate meditative concentration without interval;
as sentient beings are no longer born there, the kalpa of destruction then begins in the First Dhyāna.
The three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals are all exhausted; the four continents of Kuru, Videha, Godānīya, and Jambudvīpa;

the four kings’ heaven and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; and the six heavens of the desire realm are successively abandoned, beginning from the Avīci hell and ending with Paranirmita-vaśavartin. This process takes nineteen intermediate kalpas of increase and decrease.
When the lower realms have become empty and devoid of sentient beings, the sun’s heat increases fourfold beyond its usual intensity;
the ditches and ponds dry up, and the grasses and trees wither. When two or three suns appear, the great rivers and streams are exhausted;
when four or five appear, the oceans and springs are depleted; and when six or seven arise, even the mountains and rocks melt away.
At that time, the great earth and its blazing radiance, along with the three-thousandfold world system, became a mass of fierce fire;
flames surged upward, reaching as far as the Brahma-world. The various devas fled toward the Second Dhyāna heaven, while the Brahmakāyika and Mahābrahmā devas ascended in succession.
The entire three-thousandfold world system was reduced to ashes.

From the arising of fire from the earth until the departure of the Brahmā King, Subsequently, after one period of increase and decrease, nineteen [such periods] are reckoned as the destruction of sentient beings;
One kalpa, according to the "fewer" calculation, concerns only the receptacle world.
From this point, space is like a black pit, And remains so for twenty periods of increase and decrease.
When this period of emptiness has passed, the kalpa of formation arises. When the Great Brahmā King first establishes his solitary dwelling, one cycle of increase and decrease elapses.

From the thought of having subjects to assist sentient beings, the four heavens of the desire realm, the heavens of the four formless concentrations, and the physical world all come into being together. From that point on, they are established in successive order.
At the lower limit, a subtle wind begins to stir; celestial immortals proclaim that the kalpa is now forming.
Thus, through successive stages, a great wind arises—solid as a diamond, indestructible, its lateral breadth beyond calculation, and its perimeter shaped like a cooking tripod.
With a depth of sixteen lakṣas, beneath this wind-wheel at the base of the world,
from the Clouds of the Golden Treasury in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
rain falls in a continuous drizzle like axle-rolls, pouring down in torrents until the great trichiliocosm is filled.
Below the eight *loka-dhātus*, the remaining water solidifies; the Vajra [ground] is three hundred and twenty million [yojanas] thick, and its width is four times greater.
One should know that the measurements of twelve, three thousand, four hundred and fifty *yojanas* apply to the thickness of the water wheel (*jala-maṇḍala*), and its width is likewise.
Furthermore, rainwater pours down, increasing in depth and breadth;
the abodes of the sky-dwellers, in succession from above, are formed by great winds that strike and consolidate them into mountains and lands.

Mount Sumeru is composed of seven precious metals and pure water, while the other mountains and lands are formed from moisture and turbidity. Within these seven mountains, all the water is sweet and delicious.
The waters of the seas outside the four continents are brackish; the mountains and lands vary in coarseness and excellence.

At that time, the receptacle world is fully established. When the merit of the second dhyāna is exhausted, beings are born in Jambudvīpa, their bodies one thousand or two thousand feet tall, with pure and bright radiance, capable of flying through the air.
The food they consumed was the fat of the earth (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) and the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*), which were endowed with perfect fragrance and flavor and sustained the devas.
Later, as greed and rivalry gradually arose and they took more than their share, the earth-cakes disappeared and forest creepers (*vanalatā*) appeared.
Subsequently, as they vied for the forest creepers, non-glutinous rice (*śāli*) appeared. When they began to store it up, that too vanished and fragrant rice (*gandha-śāli*) grew.
As food gradually became coarse, excrement and urine were produced; at that time, the physical forms of male and female differentiated.
Due to their attachment and lustful passions, the radiance of their bodies vanished, and the world fell into darkness, losing its light.
Out of compassion, the Bodhisattvas raised the sun and moon; yet people vied with one another to take the fragrant rice, becoming greedy for the benefits of the earth.
Thereupon, theft first began to be practiced; together they established landowners and set boundary markers, so that the limits of fields were known and distributed evenly.

The landowners became arrogant and oppressed the weak, leading to the emergence of military formations, punishments, and the arising of killing, lying, sexual misconduct, and frivolous speech in abundance.
When the ten non-virtues are fully committed, one falls after death into the realms of ghosts, animals, or the Avīci hell;

having beheld these miserable destinies, no goodness arises. In the three continents of Uttarakuru, Pūrvavideha, and Aparagoyānī, as well as among the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and those dwelling in the celestial palaces, one gradually attains birth there by cultivating the causes.
At that time, the kalpa of formation concludes; beginning from the Brahmā King and ending with the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, both sentient beings and their physical environment are fully established.
The three kalpas of formation, destruction, and emptiness each last for twenty intermediate kalpas of increase and decrease;
during one such period of increase and decrease, a single sentient being appears in the Avīci Hell.

The retribution received by the Dragon Kings is likewise so; The Brahmakāyika gods comprise twenty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa), And the Brahmapurohita gods are comprised of forty intermediate kalpas.

One should know that for the Mahābrahmā gods, it is sixty intermediate kalpas, Because they are first born [there] and later abandon [that state]. Days, months, years, and seasons are all subsumed within the small kalpa.
The two, four, six, and eight [kalpas] are subsumed within the intermediate kalpas; the time of eighty such [intermediate] kalpas is called a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
The calamities of water, fire, and wind proceed in succession. After seven calamities of fire, there is one calamity of water;
between seven calamities of fire, there are seven calamities of water. The first and second dhyānas are respectively consumed by fire and swept away by water.
The calamity of wind can destroy the third dhyāna; In the fourth meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there is nothing that can destroy it.
Fire, water, and wind are reckoned as calamities, But their number cannot reach the measure of an *asaṃkhyeya*.
These three *asaṃkhyeyas* constitute a great eon (*mahākalpa*); When a Bodhisattva is about to ascend to perfect enlightenment, [he completes them].
The Verses on the Chapter on Kalpas (End)
